questions.q: In the lesson's four-question method, what is the first question used to classify a new quantum project ticket?
options: Is there an iterative feedback loop between a classical optimizer and a quantum circuit, or is the answer meant to come from one circuit execution?
How much will the cloud provider charge per month?
Which programming language will the team use?
How many engineers are available to staff the project?
questions.explain: The first question determines Pattern A (iterative loop) vs. Pattern B (one-shot circuit), which drives every subsequent decision about team skills, cost model, and feasibility.

questions.q: For Ticket 1 (loan risk classifier), the lesson computes a naive per-sample training loop at 130,000 circuit evaluations. What was the correct response to this number?
options: Flag it back to the proposer as a cost red flag and redesign the training approach (e.g., batching, subsampling, simulator-first development) rather than running it as-is
Immediately cancel the project since 130,000 is too large a number for any quantum project
Ignore it, since circuit evaluation counts don't affect project cost
Switch the problem to Pattern B to avoid the evaluation count issue
questions.explain: A large evaluation-count estimate is a signal to redesign the training loop's efficiency (batching, subsampling, simulator-first development), not a reason to abandon a Pattern A project or ignore the number.

questions.q: Why does the lesson classify Ticket 2 (Grover's search over 10 million records, in production next quarter) as not buildable on current hardware?
options: The qubit count (~24) and the circuit-depth requirement (~3,162 repetitions of the oracle/diffusion operators at low error) exceed what current NISQ hardware can execute reliably
Grover's algorithm is purely theoretical and has never been implemented on any hardware
Search problems are never a valid use case for quantum computing
AWS Braket and IBM Quantum do not currently offer any gate-based QPUs
questions.explain: The required qubit count and the number of oracle/diffusion repetitions needed to extract a reliable signal exceed current NISQ hardware's reliable operating range -- the lesson's honest answer is to say so explicitly rather than quietly scope down to a toy demo.

questions.q: What distinguishes a 'strong answer' from a 'weak answer' when evaluating a new quantum project ticket, according to the lesson?
options: A strong answer applies the four-question method, estimates evaluation counts, and is willing to say a problem isn't buildable at the proposed scale; a weak answer jumps straight to a yes/no verdict
A strong answer always says yes, quantum can solve the problem
A strong answer never involves any arithmetic
A strong answer always recommends Pattern B regardless of the problem
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly contrasts a structured, evidence-based walkthrough (with an honest 'not buildable at this scale' when warranted) against a reflexive yes/no judgment that skips the analysis.

questions.q: Applying the four-question method to 'use quantum computing to speed up our nightly SQL batch ETL job,' what is the most defensible response?
options: This ticket doesn't name any of the three things QPUs are actually good at (cost-function evaluation, hard sampling, specific state preparation) -- it should be flagged as likely not a quantum problem at all, rather than forced into either pattern
This is clearly Pattern A, since all production systems are Pattern A
This is clearly Pattern B, since ETL jobs run once and return a result
This should be approved immediately since quantum computing speeds up all forms of batch processing
questions.explain: Question 2 of the method asks what specifically the QPU would do. A bulk, I/O-bound SQL ETL job doesn't match cost-function evaluation, hard sampling, or specialized state preparation -- the honest response is that this isn't a quantum-shaped problem, not forcing it into a pattern.
